q-161657.name: Question 3
q-161657.problem:
Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,1\le z\le 3,\,0\le x\le 2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\}.
$$
q-161657.worked_solution:
Notice that we have a three-dimensional type II region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,{[{z}^{2}]}_{z=1}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy \\  & =8[-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /2} \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-161741.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14219559/assets/7c1738e97bc16a32f86d6901136afc4d9e288035d170fcd640db340ad36d19c5.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z\},
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane.

To find the top boundary curve of $D$ in the form $z=z(y),$ we substitute $x=1$ into the equation $x=2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z:$

$$
1=2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z\,⟹\,z=2-\frac{2}{3}y
$$

Then, we have

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2-\frac{2}{3}y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14219559/assets/ea8b8397163309a11aa478fcc21ab53ee293c19f0d77a93b5c3d3472bb0eba70.png)

Hence, the type II representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2-\frac{2}{3}y,\,\,0\le x\le 2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z\}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3-z/2}dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2-y/3-z/2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}(2-\frac{y}{3}-\frac{z}{2})-0\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}2-\frac{y}{3}-\frac{z}{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[(2-\frac{y}{3})z-\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=2-2y/3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}((2-\frac{y}{3})(2-\frac{2y}{3})-\frac{1}{4}{(2-\frac{2y}{3})}^{2})-0\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(2-\frac{2y}{3})((2-\frac{y}{3})-\frac{1}{4}(2-\frac{2y}{3}))\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(2-\frac{2y}{3})(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{6})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}3-\frac{4y}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}\,dy \\  & ={[3y-\frac{2{y}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{27}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =(3(3)-\frac{2(3)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{3}^{3}}{27})-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161680.name: Question 13
q-161680.problem: Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the planes $x=1-y$ and $x=y+1,$ and the planes $y=1,$ $y=2,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$
q-161680.worked_solution:
Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,1-y\le x\le y+1\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-y}^{y+1}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{x=1-y}^{x=y+1}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y+1-(1-y)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2y[z]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & ={2}^{2}-{1}^{2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

q-38895.name: Question 14
q-38895.problem: Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the $xy$-plane, the surface $z=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ and the planes $x=0,$ $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ $y=0,$ $y=1.$
q-38895.worked_solution:
Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[z]_{z=0}^{z=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x(\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-40319.name: Question 16
q-40319.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloids $x=5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ and the parabolic cylinder $x=9-4{y}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{a(y)}^{b(y)}\,f(y,z)\,dz\,dy
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
q-40319.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =9-4{y}^{2} \\ 9{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le x\le 9-4{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $9{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}^{9-4{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(9-4{y}^{2})-(5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}},$

for $-1\le y\le 1.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}}}\,9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}})}^{2}+(9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) \\  & =(9-9{y}^{2})+(9-9{y}^{2})+(9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) \\  & =27-27{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161703.name: Question 17
q-161703.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloids $z=2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}$ and $z=4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{a(x)}^{b(x)}\,f(x,y)\,dy\,dx
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
q-161703.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xy$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xy$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\le z\le 4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}}^{4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\text{d}z]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})-(2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $y=-\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $y=\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}},$

for $-1\le x\le 1.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}}}\,2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+(2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =(2-2{x}^{2})+(2-2{x}^{2})+(2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =6-6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-163221.name: Question 18
q-163221.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloids $z=1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and $z=3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}/2}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{\int }_{a(x)}^{b(x)}\,f(x,y)\,dy\,dx
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
q-163221.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xy$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\ 4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =2 \\ 2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xy$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le z\le 3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}^{3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\text{d}z]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})-(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $y=-\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $y=\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}},$

for $-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\le x\le \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}/2}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}}}\,2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+(2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =(1-2{x}^{2})+(1-2{x}^{2})+(2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =4-8{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161716.name: Question 19
q-161716.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the parabolic cylinders $y=4{x}^{2}$ and $y=1-2{z}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{a(x)}^{b(x)}\,f(x,z)\,dz\,dx
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
q-161716.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =1-2{z}^{2} \\ 4{x}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,4{x}^{2}\le y\le 1-2{z}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the elipse $4{x}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=1.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{4{x}^{2}}^{1-2{z}^{2}}\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{z}^{2})-(4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}},$

for $-\frac{1}{2}\le x\le \frac{1}{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{(1-4{x}^{2})/2}}^{\sqrt{(1-4{x}^{2})/2}}\,1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+(1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}+(1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =2-8{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161706.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloid $x=3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}$ and the parabolic cylinder $x=1-{y}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{a(y)}^{b(y)}\,f(y,z)\,dz\,dy
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
q-161706.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =1-{y}^{2} \\ 4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is a circle.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}\le x\le 1-{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the circle ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}^{1-{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-{y}^{2})-(3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}},$

for $-\frac{1}{2}\le y\le \frac{1}{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}}/2}^{\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}}/2}\,1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}})}^{2}+(1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1-4{y}^{2})+\frac{1}{4}(1-4{y}^{2})+(1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-6{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
